<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
Sections 1–5 of this Comment are a valuable correction of the Halden pilot, and most of their arithmetic checks out:

- **Table 2:** each gain matches its output and hours figures: 95.1/0.8 → +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 → +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 → +10.8%.
- **Hours ratios:** 34.6/40.3 is a 14.1% fall, and 34.8/40.4 is a 13.9% fall.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014/1.041 is about −2.6%.
- **Attrition:** the finding that seven of the nine withdrawals came *after* the schedule began is important. It contradicts the working paper's account of withdrawals "during the preparation phase."

The conclusion, however, goes well beyond what the analysis shows. The Comment also applies its standards selectively.

## 1. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the Comment's own numbers

- After every correction it makes, a **+10.8%** gain per actual hour remains. That is less than half the reported figure, but it is not zero.
- The abstract says the four problems account for "most" of the gain. The conclusion says "entirely." These can't both be right, and only "most" fits the evidence.
- The abstract says the 10.8% comes from "correcting the first three" problems, which include attrition. Table 2 doesn't correct for attrition at all; it adjusts only output and hours. The attrition argument is qualitative, so its effect on the estimate is unknown.
- Getting from 10.8% to zero rests entirely on the novelty argument in section 6. That argument is the weakest part of the paper (see point 3).

## 2. The randomised evidence is cited selectively

The Comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." But Varden's **case-processing** stratum, in the same trial and with the same design, found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. That result already meets almost every standard the Comment recommends:

- randomised comparison group;
- record-based output;
- timesheet hours;
- nine months of follow-up, longer than Halden's six;
- no attrition at the level of offices.

Its size is very close to the Comment's corrected 10.8%. A conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely" artifactual has to deal with this result, and the Comment doesn't mention it. The accurate synthesis is roughly this: corrected estimates converge on a per-hour gain of about 10–13% in backlog-type work, and there is a real loss of output where output depends on staff being present.

## 3. The novelty argument is weak and avoids the direct test

- **Proxy.** It infers productivity decay from *self-reported energy*. Energy is not output, and section 2 itself rejects a subjective measure (the manager-reported index) as unreliable. The Comment then relies on another subjective measure to reach its own conclusion.
- **Extrapolation.** It fits a straight line through two points. The extrapolation is also slightly off: a fall from 0.61 at month 3 to 0.29 at month 6 reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten." Either way, the trajectory could just as easily level off as keep falling.
- **The test it didn't run.** The output index was collected *monthly*, and the authors hold the microdata. Time-tracking logs give monthly hours for 27 organisations. The direct test is whether output per actual hour declines from month to month, and the Comment doesn't do it.
- **Burden of proof.** It argues that six months "is not long enough to distinguish" novelty from a durable effect, and that the burden of proof lies with those claiming durability. Both points support "undetermined," not "entirely artifact." Claiming the effect is zero is itself a claim that needs evidence.
- **Conflict with Varden.** At nine months Varden still shows a randomised per-hour gain. That is past the point at which the Comment's own extrapolation puts energy back at baseline.

## 4. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

The Comment attributes the gap between the 20% cut in scheduled hours and the actual cut to two things: +0.7 hours per day on the four remaining days, and 1.6 hours per week on the day off.

- Four days at +0.7 hours is 2.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours gives 4.4 extra hours on top of a 32-hour schedule, about **36.4 hours a week**.
- The reported pilot average is **34.6 hours**. If 1.6 hours were worked on the day off, the remaining 1.0 hour spread over four days implies about **+0.25 hours per day**, not +0.7.

Either one of the two components is wrong, or "+0.7 hours" is measured against some unstated reference. This should be resolved, because the hours correction is the largest single adjustment in Table 2.

## 5. The record-based output measure isn't clean either

"Billable hours delivered" counts time sold, so it is partly a measure of input. When hours are cut, billable hours fall almost automatically. Any rise in the value delivered per billable hour wouldn't show up, because billing rates didn't change. For professional-services organisations, the record-based index may therefore *understate* output.

The Comment should also:
- report the 23-organisation comparison broken down by type of record;
- state whether its means are weighted by employees, as the pilot's were, or unweighted. Mixing the two would distort the 3.8-point gap.

## 6. The meetings section mischaracterises Varden

- **Not a selected subgroup.** Varden's meetings correlation covers *all* treated case-processing offices. That stratum was pre-specified, so it is not "a subgroup... selected for analysis after the results were known." The data collection was unregistered, which is a fair criticism, but the subgroup wasn't chosen after the fact.
- **Varden already said this.** Varden's own text says the analysis can't establish a mechanism, and it registered a confirmatory test. "Should not be cited as a mechanism" is what Varden already said, so the section argues against a position nobody took.
- **Double standard.** The novelty argument in section 6 is at least as post hoc as the meetings analysis: two data points from an unregistered extrapolation. Yet it is the account the Comment's conclusion rests on.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Attrition bounds.** The Comment holds the microdata and could bound the attrition effect, for example by assuming the nine leavers had zero per-hour gain (an output index of 80) and weighting by their staff numbers. That would turn the argument in section 1 into a number. Note also that the five organisations that reverted after the pilot are a second, separate layer of attrition.
- **Deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for organisations' revenue; producer or sector price indices would fit better. Non-profit revenue, such as grants and donations, shouldn't be deflated as if it were sales at all. The broad point, that nominal revenue growth of 1.4% was flat or negative in real terms, still holds.
- **Retail sample size.** The retail record-based figure (−11.2%) rests on three organisations. Even so, if retail actual hours fell by about 14% like the other organisations, output per actual hour would be about +3% (88.8/0.86). That fits "output falls where it depends on presence," but not "per-hour gains are entirely an artifact."
- **Survivor subsets.** The Data note honestly says the corrected subsets aren't random. That caveat should appear in the abstract and conclusion too, since the 10.8% describes self-selected survivors who also kept good records.

## Overall

Sections 1–5 should stand, and they reinforce what Varden found by a different route: scheduled-hours denominators and manager ratings substantially overstate the gains. The defensible conclusion is:

> Corrected per-hour gains are roughly half those reported, around 10–13% in backlog-type work, consistent with the Varden case-processing stratum. Whether they persist beyond six to nine months is unresolved. Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

"Entirely an artifact" should go. If the authors want to make the novelty case, they should run the month-by-month output-per-hour analysis that their data allows. Without it, the claim is a guess.

I can draft a reply or a referee report on the Comment, or a short synthesis across all three papers.
